name: Long-duration energy storage
summary: Storage technologies hold electricity or energy for extended periods so grids can bridge longer renewable shortfalls.
useCase: A utility charges storage during plentiful generation and discharges it over a long evening, overnight period or multi-day event.
whyNow: Non-lithium storage deployments are growing, but competitive economics and funding remain difficult. Published deployment figures often classify technology families rather than strictly counting systems that discharge for ten hours or more.

mainstream.scope: Routine procurement of eight-to-100-hour storage for selected grid and industrial needs where duration has an explicit economic value.
mainstream.rationale: Greater renewable exposure creates use cases, but lithium-ion remains a formidable competitor over shorter durations. Contracts that pay for prolonged availability, rather than only energy throughput, are essential. Some chemistries may not scale by 2035.

metric.name: Annual deployment of non-lithium long-duration technology families
metric.scope: Wood Mackenzie category including compressed air, thermal and flow batteries; not a strict ten-hour asset census
metric.limitations: 2025 was reported as more than 15 GWh, up 49%; the approximately 10.1 GWh 2024 point is back-calculated and rounded, not an independently reported exact count. Some included flow and compressed-air assets average about four hours, so this is a technology-family proxy. It must not be labelled a census of all ten-hour-plus storage.
metric.futureNote: No defensible like-for-like external forecast is available for this KPI. The forward maturity path is a separately labelled analyst scenario, not a numerical adoption forecast.
metric.growthLabel: Reported installations grew 49% in 2025; category includes some shorter-duration systems.

milestones.text: US Department of Energy launched its Storage Shot cost-reduction goal for long-duration storage; a goal is not an achieved cost reduction.
No comparable 2022 deployment point is included.
No comparable 2023 deployment point is included.
The approximate 2024 baseline is back-calculated from the subsequently reported growth rate; it should not be presented as exact measured GWh.
Wood Mackenzie reports more than 15 GWh of installations across the relevant technology families, up 49%.
The March 2026 report also describes funding constraints; this is a completed-2025 deployment figure, not a 2026 annual estimate.

tailwinds: Renewable-heavy grids need flexibility across longer intervals
Industrial heat storage can serve a different market from electricity batteries
bottlenecks: Lithium-ion cost and established financing over shorter durations
Low cycling frequency can weaken project revenue
First commercial projects carry execution and counterparty risk
watchMetrics: Operating GWh separated by discharge duration and chemistry
Contracted revenue, availability and realised round-trip efficiency
Construction cost, commissioning dates and finance secured
